topics.description: Classes, the four OOP pillars, the five SOLID rules and how to draw a quick UML class diagram.
topics.revision_note_md:
## OOP & SOLID

- **Encapsulation** (hide data behind methods), **Abstraction** (expose what, hide how), **Inheritance** (is-a), **Polymorphism** (same call, different behaviour).
- **SOLID**: Single responsibility · Open/closed · Liskov substitution · Interface segregation · Dependency inversion.
- Prefer **composition (has-a)** over inheritance.

lesson.simple:
Low-level design (LLD) interviews check whether you can turn a real-world problem into **clean classes**. Three building blocks:

1. **OOP pillars** — wrap data with the methods that change it (encapsulation); hide details behind simple methods (abstraction); share behaviour (inheritance); let different classes answer the same method call in their own way (polymorphism).
2. **SOLID** — five rules that keep classes small and easy to extend.
3. **UML class diagram** — boxes for classes, lines for relationships. You'll start every LLD round by drawing one.
lesson.analogy: A restaurant: the waiter (interface) takes your order without you knowing how the kitchen works (abstraction). The chef, the cashier and the cleaner each have one job (single responsibility). Adding a new dish doesn't mean rebuilding the kitchen (open/closed).

concepts.title: The four OOP pillars, with the 'why'
concepts.body:
- **Encapsulation** — keep an object's data private and change it only through its methods. A `BankAccount` exposes `deposit()` and `withdraw()`, not a writable `balance`, so the rule *"balance can't go negative"* lives in one place and can't be bypassed.
- **Abstraction** — show *what* an object does, hide *how*. Callers use `PaymentMethod.pay(amount)` without knowing whether it's UPI, card or wallet.
- **Inheritance** — a subclass reuses and extends a parent (`SavingsAccount(Account)`). Powerful, but it couples the classes tightly; a change in the parent ripples to every child.
- **Polymorphism** — different classes respond to the same method call in their own way. `for p in payments: p.pay(100)` works for every payment type, and adding a new type needs no change to the loop.

In LLD rounds the pillars aren't asked as definitions; they show up as design choices. Private fields + validation (encapsulation), interfaces for things that vary (abstraction + polymorphism), and inheritance only for true "is-a" relationships.

concepts.title: SOLID, one example each
concepts.body:
| Principle | Rule of thumb | Violation → fix |
|---|---|---|
| **S**ingle Responsibility | a class has one reason to change | `Invoice` that calculates, prints *and* emails → split into `Invoice`, `InvoicePrinter`, `InvoiceMailer` |
| **O**pen/Closed | add behaviour by adding code, not editing working code | `if type == 'upi' … elif 'card'` in checkout → a `PaymentMethod` interface, one class per type |
| **L**iskov Substitution | a subclass must work anywhere its parent does | `Square(Rectangle)` breaks `set_width` expectations → don't inherit; share an interface |
| **I**nterface Segregation | small, focused interfaces | `Machine` with `print/scan/fax` forces a basic printer to fake `fax` → `Printer`, `Scanner` interfaces |
| **D**ependency Inversion | depend on abstractions, inject them | `OrderService` creating `MySQLRepo()` inside → take an `OrderRepository` in the constructor |

Dependency inversion is the one that makes code **testable**: pass in a fake repository or a fixed clock in tests.

concepts.title: Composition over inheritance
concepts.body:
Inheritance says **"is-a"** (a `Car` is a `Vehicle`); composition says **"has-a"** (a `Car` has an `Engine`). Prefer composition when behaviour varies independently.

Imagine ducks: `FlyingDuck`, `QuackingDuck`, `FlyingQuackingDuck`, `RubberDuck`… With inheritance, every combination needs a class. With composition, a `Duck` **has** a `FlyBehaviour` and a `QuackBehaviour`; you plug in `FlyWithWings` or `NoFly` at construction time. That's the Strategy pattern, and it's why most patterns are built on composition.

Use inheritance when:
- the relationship is genuinely "is-a" and stable,
- subclasses pass Liskov (they can stand in for the parent),
- you're sharing real code, not just a type (otherwise an interface/ABC is enough).

concepts.title: Reading and drawing a UML class diagram
concepts.body:
Each class is a box with three parts: **name**, **fields** (`- balance: int`), **methods** (`+ deposit(amount): void`). `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected.

Relationships, from weakest to strongest:

| Relationship | Meaning | Example | Drawn as |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dependency** | uses temporarily | `Checkout` uses a `Coupon` in one method | dashed arrow |
| **Association** | knows about, long-term | `Member` — `Loan` | solid line (with multiplicity 1, *, 0..1) |
| **Aggregation** | has-a, parts can live alone | `Team` ◇— `Player` | hollow diamond |
| **Composition** | owns, parts die with the whole | `Order` ◆— `OrderLine` | filled diamond |
| **Inheritance** | is-a | `Car` —▷ `Vehicle` | hollow triangle |
| **Realisation** | implements an interface | `UpiPayment` ┄▷ `PaymentMethod` | dashed line + triangle |

In an interview, nobody checks perfect notation. They check that you found the right **classes**, **responsibilities** and **multiplicities** (one floor has many spots) before writing code.

topics.name: Core Design Patterns
topics.description: Strategy, Observer, Factory, Singleton and State — what problem each solves and how to spot it.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Five patterns to know cold

| Pattern | Use when | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy | swap an algorithm at runtime | pricing, payment, sorting |
| Observer | many listeners react to an event | notifications, stock ticker |
| Factory | create objects without hard-coding the class | NotificationFactory |
| Singleton | exactly one shared instance | config, logger, DB pool |
| State | behaviour depends on current state | vending machine, elevator |

lesson.simple:
Design patterns are **named solutions to common design problems**. You don't need all 23 — five cover most LLD interviews:

- **Strategy** — put each algorithm in its own class behind one interface; pick one at runtime.
- **Observer** — a subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies them all when something happens.
- **Factory** — one place decides which concrete class to create.
- **Singleton** — one shared instance (use sparingly).
- **State** — each state is a class; the object delegates behaviour to its current state, and states switch it to the next one.
lesson.analogy: Strategy is Google Maps letting you pick car, bike or walking — same 'get route' call, different algorithm. Observer is a YouTube subscription: upload once, every subscriber gets notified.

concepts.title: Strategy: swap an algorithm without touching the caller
concepts.body:
**Problem:** a class has several ways to do one thing (pricing, sorting, routing, discount rules), and you keep adding `if/elif` branches.

**Solution:** define an interface (`PricingStrategy.price(ticket)`), put each variant in its own class, and give the context object a strategy at construction (or let it switch at runtime).

**How to spot it in an LLD prompt:** words like *"different ways to…"*, *"configurable"*, *"rules may change"*: payment methods, parking pricing, elevator dispatch, rate-limiting algorithms, notification channels.

**Trade-off:** more small classes, but each one is easy to test and adding a variant never edits existing code (Open/Closed).

concepts.title: Factory and Singleton: controlling creation
concepts.body:
**Factory** puts the "which concrete class?" decision in one place. Instead of `if kind == 'car': Car() …` scattered across the code, call `VehicleFactory.create(kind)`. Adding a new type touches one function. A **registry dict** (`{'car': Car, 'bike': Bike}`) is the idiomatic Python version.

**Singleton** guarantees one instance (a config, a connection pool, a logger). In Python a module-level object is already a singleton; in Java you'd use a private constructor plus a static instance (with thread-safe lazy init).

Use Singleton **sparingly**: it's global state in disguise, it hides dependencies, and it makes tests share state. Interviewers like hearing: *"I'd make it a single instance created at startup and inject it, rather than calling `getInstance()` everywhere."*

concepts.title: State: let each state handle the inputs
concepts.body:
**Problem:** an object behaves differently depending on its state (vending machine: idle / has money / dispensing; order: placed / paid / shipped / delivered), and every method is a growing `if state == …` ladder.

**Solution:** one class per state, all implementing the same methods (`insert_coin`, `select`, `dispense`). The context delegates to its current state object; each state decides what the input means *in that state* and switches the context to the next state.

**State vs Strategy:** they look the same in code (an interface plus several implementations). The difference is *who changes it*: a Strategy is chosen from outside and usually stays; States **replace themselves** as the object moves through its lifecycle.

Draw the **state diagram** first (states as circles, inputs as arrows). It doubles as your test plan: every arrow is a test case, every missing arrow is an invalid action to reject.

concepts.title: Other patterns worth recognising
concepts.body:
You won't need to implement these often, but naming them correctly impresses:

- **Decorator** — wrap an object to add behaviour without subclassing: `LoggingPayment(UpiPayment())`, late fee on top of base pricing, coffee + milk + sugar.
- **Adapter** — make an incompatible class fit your interface: wrap a third-party payment SDK so it looks like your `PaymentMethod`.
- **Builder** — construct complex objects step by step with readable code: `Pizza.builder().size('L').add('olives').build()`.
- **Command** — wrap a request as an object, enabling queues, undo and retry (text editor undo, job schedulers).
- **Chain of Responsibility** — pass a request along a chain of handlers until one handles it (ATM dispensing ₹500, then ₹200, then ₹100 notes; middleware).
- **Facade** — one simple entry point over a complex subsystem (`BookingService` hiding seat, payment and notification services).

topics.description: SOLID, design patterns and classic machine-coding LLD rounds: parking lot, elevator, Splitwise.
topics.revision_note_md:
## LLD round approach

1. Clarify scope and list **use cases**.
2. Identify **entities** (nouns) and **behaviours** (verbs).
3. Draw a class diagram: relationships (has-a vs is-a), enums for states.
4. Apply **SOLID** and a pattern where it removes an `if/else` chain (Strategy, Factory, Observer, State).
5. Write clean, runnable code for the core flow; handle concurrency if asked.

**SOLID**: Single responsibility · Open/closed · Liskov substitution · Interface segregation · Dependency inversion.

items.title: Explain SOLID principles with examples
hints: Give one bad and one good example for each.
Strategy pattern is open/closed in action.
items.explanation: Single responsibility: one reason to change; Open-closed: extend without modifying; Liskov: subtypes must be substitutable; Interface segregation: small focused interfaces; Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions.
items.answer_md:
- **S** — `Invoice` shouldn't also print and email itself.
- **O** — add a new `PaymentMethod` class instead of editing a giant `switch`.
- **L** — `Square extends Rectangle` breaks setters → violates Liskov.
- **I** — split `Worker{work(); eat()}` so robots don't implement `eat`.
- **D** — `OrderService` takes a `PaymentGateway` interface, not a concrete `StripeClient`.

items.title: Design a parking lot
items.explanation: Entities: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot by type, Vehicle by type, Ticket, Payment; use a strategy for spot allocation and pricing, and lock spot assignment for concurrency.
items.answer_md:
Classes: `ParkingLot` → `Floor[]` → `Spot(type, isFree)`; `Vehicle(type)`; `Ticket(spot, entryTime)`; `EntryGate/ExitGate`; `PricingStrategy` (hourly, flat); `SpotAllocationStrategy` (nearest first).

Flow: vehicle arrives → find spot (strategy) → issue ticket → exit → compute fee → pay → free spot. Mention thread-safety when two gates grab the same spot.

items.title: Design Splitwise (expense sharing)
hints: How do you minimise the number of transactions?
items.explanation: Model User, Group, Expense with split strategies (equal, exact, percent), maintain a balance map per user pair, and simplify debts with a greedy max-creditor/max-debtor algorithm.
items.answer_md:
Entities: `User`, `Group`, `Expense(paidBy, amount, splits)`, `Split` (Equal/Exact/Percent via **Strategy**), `BalanceSheet` (net amount per user).

**Simplify debts:** compute net balance per user; repeatedly match the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor (heaps) until all are zero.

items.title: Which design patterns come up most in interviews?
hints: Pick a real system for each pattern.
Singleton is often called an anti-pattern — know why.
items.explanation: Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Builder and State — know a one-line purpose and a real example for each.
items.answer_md:
- **Factory** — create objects without exposing the concrete class (`NotificationFactory.create('sms')`).
- **Strategy** — swap algorithms at runtime (pricing, sorting, payment).
- **Observer** — pub/sub (event listeners, stock ticker).
- **Decorator** — add behaviour by wrapping (middleware, Java I/O streams).
- **Builder** — construct complex objects step by step.
- **State** — vending machine / elevator states.
- **Singleton** — one instance (config, logger); hurts testability.

topics.name: LLD Build: Parking Lot
topics.description: The most-asked LLD problem: floors, spot types, tickets, pricing strategy and concurrent spot allocation.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Parking Lot — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: vehicle types, spot types, multiple floors/gates, pricing, payment.
2. UML: ParkingLot → Floor → Spot; Vehicle; Ticket; Gate; PricingStrategy; SpotAllocationStrategy.
3. Core flow: enter → allocate spot → ticket → exit → price → pay → free spot.
4. Concurrency: two gates must never get the same spot → lock per spot type / atomic allocation.

lesson.simple:
Design a parking lot that issues tickets, finds a free spot of the right size, and charges on exit.

**Keep it simple first**: one floor, three spot sizes, hourly pricing. **Then extend**: multiple floors, entry/exit gates, different pricing, EV charging.

The parts interviewers care about most: clean classes, a **strategy** for pricing and spot allocation, and **how you stop two gates from giving away the same spot**.
lesson.analogy: A mall parking attendant with a clipboard of free spots per size. If two attendants share one clipboard, they must take turns writing on it — that's the lock.

concepts.title: Requirements first: what to clarify
concepts.body:
Spend two minutes turning the vague prompt into a list. Typical questions and sensible defaults:

- **Vehicle types?** Bike, car, truck (maybe EV). **Spot types?** Small, compact, large (maybe EV with charger).
- **Can a small vehicle use a bigger spot?** Usually yes if its own type is full — say it.
- **Floors and gates?** Multiple floors, several entry and exit gates working at the same time.
- **Pricing?** Hourly by vehicle type, first hour free, flat weekend rate… → must be changeable.
- **Payment?** Cash, card, UPI at the exit gate or a kiosk.
- **Out of scope:** reservations, monthly passes, admin dashboards — mention them as extensions.

Then list the use cases you'll actually code: **park (issue ticket)**, **exit (pay and free the spot)**, **show free spots per floor**.

concepts.title: Concurrency: two gates, one spot
concepts.body:
The race: gate A and gate B both read "spot C1 is free", both assign it, and two cars arrive at the same spot.

Fixes, from simplest to most scalable:
1. **One lock around allocation** — simple and correct; contention is fine for a few gates.
2. **A lock per spot type or per floor** — gates allocating different types don't block each other.
3. **Atomic pop from a thread-safe structure** — a concurrent queue of free spots per type; `pop` is atomic.
4. **In a database** — `UPDATE spots SET occupied = true WHERE id = :id AND occupied = false`; if 0 rows changed, someone else took it — try the next spot. Or `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to grab the next free row without waiting.

Always keep the critical section small: allocate the spot inside the lock, but print the ticket, call the display board and take payment outside it.

concepts.title: Extensions interviewers ask for
concepts.body:
- **EV charging spots** — a new spot type plus a `ChargingSession` billed by kWh; pricing becomes base parking + charging (Decorator or a composite pricing strategy).
- **Display boards per floor** — Observer: floors publish "free count changed", boards subscribe.
- **Lost ticket** — look up the vehicle by plate, charge a fixed maximum fee.
- **Reservations** — a `Reservation` holds a spot for a time window; allocation must skip reserved spots.
- **Multiple lots in a city** — this becomes HLD: a central service, per-lot databases, and an API for apps to show availability.

Show that each extension mostly **adds classes** rather than editing existing ones — that's the payoff of the strategies you introduced.

topics.name: LLD Build: Vending Machine
topics.description: A State-pattern classic: idle, has-money, dispensing — inventory, change and refunds.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Vending Machine

- States: **Idle → HasMoney → Dispensing → Idle** (plus OutOfStock).
- Each state class handles: insert_coin, select_item, dispense, refund.
- Inventory: item code → (product, price, count). Return change with the fewest coins.

lesson.simple:
A vending machine reacts differently to the same button depending on what's happening: pressing *select* with no money should say "insert coins", but with enough money it should dispense.

That's exactly the **State pattern**: one class per state, each handling the inputs for that state and moving the machine to the next state. No giant if/else.
lesson.analogy: A traffic light: the same 'timer ticked' event turns green → yellow, yellow → red, red → green. Each colour knows what comes next.

concepts.title: Draw the state diagram before any code
concepts.body:
States and the inputs that move between them:

```text
        insert coin               select (enough money, in stock)
IDLE ───────────────▶ HAS_MONEY ─────────────────────────────▶ DISPENSING
  ▲                    │   │ insert coin (stays)                    │
  │   cancel / refund  │   │ select (not enough / out of stock):    │
  └────────────────────┘   │   stay, show message                   │
  ▲                                                                 │
  └─────────────────────── item dropped, change returned ───────────┘
```

Every arrow becomes a method on a state class; every input that has **no arrow** from a state (e.g. *select* in IDLE) must be handled politely: show a message, don't crash, don't change state. Add a **MAINTENANCE / OUT_OF_SERVICE** state if the prompt mentions restocking.

concepts.title: Money, change and inventory details
concepts.body:
- **Store money as integers** (paise or the smallest coin), never floats — `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`.
- **Inventory:** a map from slot code to `(product, price, count)`. Check stock *before* taking the money for that item.
- **Making change** with limited coins: try the largest denominations first (greedy), but with arbitrary coin sets greedy can fail — then you'd need DP. Mention it; real machines refuse the sale ("exact change only") if change can't be made.
- **Refund on cancel:** return the inserted amount, ideally with the same coins.
- **Atomic dispense:** decrement stock, deduct price and return change as one step; if the motor fails, refund and move to OUT_OF_SERVICE.

topics.name: LLD Build: Rate Limiter
topics.description: Limit how many requests each client can make: token bucket vs sliding window, a strategy per algorithm, and thread safety.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Rate Limiter — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: limit per user / API key / IP; per endpoint config; what happens on reject (HTTP 429 + Retry-After).
2. Classes: `RateLimiter` (interface) → `TokenBucket`, `SlidingWindowLog`, `FixedWindow`; `RateLimiterRegistry` holds one limiter per key; `RuleConfig`.
3. Algorithms: **token bucket** allows bursts up to capacity; **sliding window** gives a smooth, exact limit.
4. Concurrency: lock per key (or atomic ops); in a cluster the state moves to Redis.

lesson.simple:
A **rate limiter** says *"you can make at most N requests in this much time"*. It protects your API from abuse and from one noisy client starving everyone else.

Two algorithms cover almost every interview:
- **Token bucket** — each client has a bucket that holds up to *capacity* tokens and refills at a steady rate. A request spends one token; no token → rejected. Allows short **bursts**.
- **Sliding window log** — remember the timestamps of recent requests; allow a new one only if fewer than N happened in the last window. Exact, but uses more memory.

In LLD, show a `RateLimiter` **interface** with one class per algorithm (Strategy pattern), a registry that keeps one limiter **per client key**, and a **lock** so two threads can't both spend the last token.
lesson.analogy: A token bucket is a metro card that gets ₹1 added every second, up to a maximum of ₹3. Each ride costs ₹1. You can take three rides back to back (a burst), then you wait for it to refill.

concepts.title: The classic algorithms compared
concepts.body:
| Algorithm | How it works | Memory per client | Bursts | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed window** | count requests per clock window (e.g. per minute) | 1 counter | up to 2× at window edges | approximate |
| **Sliding window log** | keep timestamps of recent requests | O(limit) | none | exact |
| **Sliding window counter** | weighted mix of the current and previous window counts | 2 counters | small | very close |
| **Token bucket** | tokens refill at a steady rate up to a capacity; each request spends one | 2 numbers | up to capacity | exact for rate + burst |
| *(Leaky bucket)* | requests drain from a queue at a fixed rate | queue | smoothed out | exact output rate |

**Sliding window counter** formula: `estimate = current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)`. It fixes the fixed-window edge burst with almost no memory — a popular production choice.

Pick with a reason: *"APIs where short bursts are fine → token bucket; strict per-minute quotas → sliding window."*

concepts.title: Designing the classes
concepts.body:
```text
RateLimiter (interface)        allow(key) -> bool
  ├─ TokenBucketLimiter        capacity, refill_rate, buckets: key -> (tokens, last)
  ├─ SlidingWindowLogLimiter   limit, window, logs: key -> deque[timestamps]
  └─ FixedWindowLimiter
RuleConfig                     (client tier, endpoint) -> algorithm + numbers
RateLimiterFactory             builds the right limiter from a RuleConfig
Clock (injected)               now() — real or fake for tests
```

Decisions worth saying out loud:
- **Key** = user id, API key or IP (+ endpoint). Unauthenticated traffic is limited by IP.
- **Lazy refill** — compute tokens from elapsed time when a request arrives; no background timers.
- **Cleanup** — evict idle keys (LRU / TTL), or memory grows with every client ever seen.
- **Response** — HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`, plus `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers.

concepts.title: Thread safety in one process
concepts.body:
`allow()` is a **read-modify-write**: read tokens, decide, write tokens back. Two threads interleaving can both read "1 token left" and both succeed.

Options:
- **One lock per limiter** — simplest; fine for moderate traffic.
- **A lock per key** (striped locks: `locks[hash(key) % 64]`) — different users don't contend.
- **Lock-free atomics** — compare-and-swap on a packed (tokens, timestamp) value; more complex, rarely needed in an interview.

Keep the critical section tiny: only the refill-check-spend. Never do I/O (logging, DB calls) while holding the lock.

concepts.title: Going distributed
concepts.body:
With many API servers, in-memory buckets would each allow the full limit. Move state to a shared store:

- **Redis + Lua script** — the script reads tokens and timestamp, refills, checks and spends atomically in one round trip. Redis runs scripts one at a time, so no race.
- **Fixed window in Redis** — `INCR key:{minute}`; on the first increment set `EXPIRE 60`; reject if the result exceeds the limit. Two commands, cheap and good enough for many cases.
- **Latency** — one Redis round trip (~1 ms) per request; for very hot paths, use a **local token cache** that syncs with Redis in batches and accept slight over-allowance.
- **Failure mode** — if Redis is down, *fail open* (allow, protect availability) or *fail closed* (reject, protect the backend). Choose per endpoint: login → fail closed; reading a public page → fail open.

A background thread refilling every bucket every second — doesn't scale; refill lazily on each request.

quiz.why: A full bucket can be spent immediately, then refills at a steady rate.

quiz.q: Why is a lock needed in TokenBucket.allow()?

quiz.q: In a cluster of 10 API servers, the bucket state should live in…
options: A shared store like Redis, updated atomically

**Problem:** in-memory buckets on N servers allow N × the limit.

**Fix:** store state in Redis keyed by client, e.g. `rl:{client}` → `{tokens, last}`.

- Run refill + check + spend in **one Lua script** so it's atomic.
- Simpler fixed-window variant: `INCR rl:{client}:{minute}` + `EXPIRE 60`; reject when the count passes the limit.
- Return **HTTP 429** with `Retry-After`.
- If Redis is down: fail open (allow) for availability or fail closed for safety — say which and why.

topics.name: LLD Build: Elevator System
topics.description: Elevators that pick up and drop passengers efficiently: state, direction, a scheduling strategy and a controller that dispatches requests.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Elevator — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: N elevators, M floors, hall buttons (up/down) and car buttons (floor), capacity, display.
2. Classes: `ElevatorController` → `Elevator` (current floor, direction, state, stops); `Request` (floor, direction); `DispatchStrategy` (which elevator?) and `Elevator.step()` (which floor next?).
3. Scheduling: **LOOK** — keep going in one direction while there are stops ahead, then reverse.
4. Concurrency: buttons are pressed from many threads → thread-safe request queue; each elevator runs its own loop.

lesson.simple:
Design the software that runs a building's lifts. People press **hall buttons** ("I'm on floor 4, going up") and **car buttons** inside ("take me to 9").

Two decisions make the design:
1. **Which elevator** answers a hall call? (the **dispatch** strategy — e.g. nearest elevator already moving that way)
2. **Which floor next** for one elevator? (the **scheduling** rule — usually **LOOK**: keep going in the current direction while there are stops ahead, then turn around)

Model each elevator with a **state** (IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOORS_OPEN) and two sorted sets of stops: those above and those below.
lesson.analogy: A bus driver on a straight road. They pick up everyone going their way, drive to the end of the requests, then turn around — instead of zig-zagging to whoever called first.

concepts.title: Model the moving parts
concepts.body:
| Class | Holds | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `ElevatorController` | all elevators, dispatch strategy | receives hall calls, assigns an elevator |
| `Elevator` | current floor, direction, state, stops above/below, capacity | `add_stop`, `step` (move one stop), open/close doors |
| `Request` | floor, direction (hall) or target floor (car) | — |
| `DispatchStrategy` | — | choose an elevator for a hall call |
| `Door`, `Display`, `Button` | — | small parts; displays observe elevator position |

Two kinds of input:
- **Hall call** — "I'm on floor 4, going up" → the controller picks an elevator.
- **Car call** — "take me to 9", pressed inside → goes straight to *that* elevator's stops.

Elevator **states**: IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOORS_OPEN, MAINTENANCE/EMERGENCY.

concepts.title: Scheduling one elevator: FCFS, SCAN and LOOK
concepts.body:
- **First-come-first-served:** serve requests in order. Simple, but it zig-zags (2 → 9 → 3 → 8) and wastes most of its time travelling.
- **SCAN (elevator algorithm):** sweep in one direction to the **end of the building**, serving stops on the way, then reverse.
- **LOOK:** like SCAN, but reverse at the **last requested floor** instead of the building's end. This is what real elevators approximate.

Data structure: two ordered sets — stops above the current floor (served in increasing order while going up) and stops below (served in decreasing order going down). A hall call for "down" at a floor above you while you're going up is served on the way back down, not on the way up.

Starvation: with LOOK, a request in the opposite direction waits at most one full sweep, so no one waits forever.

concepts.title: Dispatching across many elevators
concepts.body:
The controller scores each elevator for a hall call `(floor, direction)` and picks the lowest score. A common scoring idea:

1. **Already moving towards the floor in the same direction** → cost = distance.
2. **Idle** → cost = distance.
3. **Moving away or in the opposite direction** → cost = distance to finish its sweep + distance back (or a big penalty).

Add tie-breakers for load (fewer stops, fewer passengers) and capacity (skip full cars). Real systems also use **zoning** (elevators A–C serve floors 1–20) and **destination dispatch** (passengers enter the target floor in the lobby, so the system groups people going to nearby floors).

Make this a `DispatchStrategy` so you can swap "nearest car" for "zoned" without touching the controller.

concepts.title: Concurrency and safety
concepts.body:
- **Inputs from many threads:** buttons on every floor and in every car fire concurrently. Each elevator's stop sets need a lock, or a single-threaded event loop per elevator that consumes a thread-safe request queue.
- **One controller loop or one per elevator?** A loop per elevator (each moves independently) plus a lock-protected dispatcher is easy to explain.
- **Safety rules belong in code, not in hope:** doors never open while moving; weight sensor blocks departure when overloaded; emergency mode overrides everything.
- **Testing:** inject a fake clock/motor, push a scripted sequence of calls, and assert the visited floor order — exactly like the dry run in this lesson.

topics.name: LLD Build: Snake & Ladders
topics.description: A playable board game model: board, snakes and ladders, dice strategy, players taking turns and a winner.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Snake & Ladders — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: board size, any number of snakes/ladders, 2+ players, dice count, win on exact 100 or not.
2. Classes: `Game` (players queue, board, dice, winner), `Board` (size, jumps map), `Dice` (strategy: random / fixed for tests), `Player`.
3. Snakes and ladders are both just a **jump**: `start → end`; one map handles both.
4. Turn loop: roll → move → apply jump → check win → next player (queue rotation).

lesson.simple:
A small but complete design: build a game you could actually play in the terminal.

The neat simplification: **snakes and ladders are the same thing** — a square that sends you somewhere else. A snake goes down, a ladder goes up. So the board just keeps one map: `jumps = {start: end}`.

Players take turns from a **queue**: pop the front player, roll, move, apply a jump if they land on one, check for a win, then push them to the back.

Make the **dice a strategy** (an interface), so tests can use a fixed sequence of rolls instead of randomness.
lesson.analogy: A board game night with a scorekeeper. The scorekeeper doesn't care if a square has a snake or a ladder drawn on it — the rule card just says "square 17 → square 7".

concepts.title: Entities and the game loop
concepts.body:
```text
Game   — board, dice, turn queue of players, positions, winner, rules
Board  — size, jumps {start: end} (snakes go down, ladders go up)
Dice   — interface: roll() → int (RandomDice, FixedDice for tests, multiple dice)
Player — id, name
```

The loop:
1. Take the player at the **front** of the queue.
2. Roll, compute the target square.
3. Apply the rules: past the last square? (stay, or bounce back). Landing on a jump? Move to its end.
4. Reached the last square → winner. Otherwise put the player at the **back** of the queue.

Keep the board **validated** at construction: no jump starts on square 1 or the last square, no jump points to its own start, no chains that loop forever (a snake ending on a ladder that leads back to it).

concepts.title: Making rules pluggable
concepts.body:
Different groups play different house rules:
- exact landing on 100 vs bounce back from 100,
- extra turn on a 6,
- three 6s in a row cancel the turn,
- start only after rolling a 6,
- two dice instead of one.

Put these behind a `RulesStrategy` (or a few small policy objects) with methods like `next_position(pos, roll)` and `gets_extra_turn(roll, streak)`. The `Game` loop asks the rules instead of hard-coding them. This is the same Open/Closed idea as pricing in the parking lot — and it's what the interviewer is really testing in this "easy" question.

concepts.title: Testability and running many games
concepts.body:
**Determinism:** randomness is the enemy of tests. Inject the dice: `FixedDice([3, 4, 5])` lets you assert exact positions after each turn, including snake and ladder hits and the winning roll. A seeded `random.Random(42)` is the other option.

**Many games on one server** (an online version): each `Game` instance owns its state, so games don't interfere. Store games in a map by id; each request (`roll` for player X in game G) loads that game, checks it's X's turn (reject out-of-turn moves), applies the turn and saves. Concurrency issue to mention: two requests for the same game at once → lock per game or optimistic versioning.

topics.description: Members borrow and return book copies, with due dates, fines and reservations — practise drawing UML before code.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Library Management — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: search catalogue, borrow/return, max books per member, due dates, fines, reservations/holds.
2. Key split: **Book** (title, author, ISBN — the idea) vs **BookItem** (one physical copy with a barcode and status).
3. Classes: `Library`, `Catalog` (search), `Member`, `Loan`, `Reservation`, `FinePolicy` (strategy), `NotificationService` (observer).
4. Rules: can't borrow a copy reserved for someone else; returning a copy with a waiting hold notifies the next member.

lesson.simple:
Members search for books, borrow a copy, return it, and pay a fine if it's late. If all copies are out, they can **reserve** one and get notified when it comes back.

The one modelling insight interviewers look for: **a Book is not a copy**. *"Clean Code"* is a `Book` (title, author, ISBN). The library owns three `BookItem`s of it, each with its own barcode and status (AVAILABLE, LOANED, RESERVED, LOST).

Draw the **UML first**: Library → Catalog → Book → BookItem; Member → Loan → BookItem; Reservation queue per Book; FinePolicy as a strategy.
lesson.analogy: A movie is not a DVD. The video shop has one entry for the film in its catalogue, and several numbered discs on the shelf — you rent a disc, not the film.

concepts.title: Turning requirements into use cases
concepts.body:
Actors: **member**, **librarian**, **system** (scheduled jobs).

| Use case | Actor | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| Search catalogue | member | by title, author, ISBN, subject |
| Borrow a copy | member / librarian | copy available (or reserved for this member); under the loan limit; no unpaid fines over a threshold |
| Return a copy | librarian | compute fine; hand to the next reservation if any |
| Reserve a title | member | only when no copy is available; FIFO queue |
| Renew a loan | member | not if someone has reserved the title |
| Send reminders | system | due tomorrow, overdue, reservation ready |
| Add/remove copies, mark lost | librarian | |

Listing use cases with their **rules** gives you the methods and the checks before you write a single class.

concepts.title: Book vs BookItem and the other key entities
concepts.body:
- **Book** — the title as an idea: ISBN, title, authors, subject. Many copies share one Book.
- **BookItem** — a physical copy: barcode, rack location, status (AVAILABLE, LOANED, RESERVED, LOST, DAMAGED).
- **Member** — id, type (student, staff — drives limits), active loans, fines owed.
- **Loan** — BookItem + Member + issue date + due date + return date.
- **Reservation** — Book (not a copy!) + Member + created time + status. A member waits for *any* copy.
- **Catalog** — search indexes (title, author, subject).
- **FinePolicy**, **LoanPolicy** — strategies by member type (staff may borrow 10 books for 30 days).
- **NotificationService** — email/SMS observers.

Reservations attach to **Book** and loans attach to **BookItem** — getting that difference right is the main thing the interviewer checks.

concepts.title: The return flow, where most rules meet
concepts.body:
When a copy comes back:
1. Find the active loan by barcode; set the return date.
2. **Fine** = `FinePolicy.fine(due, returned, member_type)`; add it to the member's balance.
3. Is anyone waiting for this **Book**? If yes, mark the copy **RESERVED for the first member in the queue**, start a pickup deadline (e.g. 3 days), and notify them. If they don't collect it in time, move to the next member.
4. Otherwise mark it AVAILABLE.

Concurrency: two members at two counters borrowing the last copy → the status change must be atomic (`UPDATE book_items SET status = 'LOANED' WHERE barcode = :b AND status = 'AVAILABLE'`).

template.python:
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date, timedelta
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    AVAILABLE = 'available'
    LOANED = 'loaned'
    RESERVED = 'reserved'

@dataclass
class Book:
    isbn: str
    title: str
    holds: deque = field(default_factory=deque)     # members waiting

@dataclass
class BookItem:
    barcode: str
    book: Book
    status: Status = Status.AVAILABLE
    reserved_for: str | None = None

@dataclass
class Loan:
    item: BookItem
    member: str
    due: date

class PerDayFine:
    def __init__(self, per_day=10): self.per_day = per_day
    def fine(self, due: date, returned: date) -> int:
        return max(0, (returned - due).days) * self.per_day

class Library:
    LOAN_DAYS, MAX_LOANS = 14, 3

    def __init__(self, fine_policy=PerDayFine(), notify=print):
        self.items: dict[str, BookItem] = {}
        self.loans: dict[str, Loan] = {}             # barcode -> loan
        self.fine_policy, self.notify = fine_policy, notify

    def add_copy(self, item: BookItem): self.items[item.barcode] = item

    def borrow(self, member: str, barcode: str, today: date) -> Loan:
        item = self.items[barcode]
        if item.status == Status.LOANED:
            raise ValueError('copy is out')
        if item.status == Status.RESERVED and item.reserved_for != member:
            raise ValueError('reserved for someone else')
        if sum(l.member == member for l in self.loans.values()) >= self.MAX_LOANS:
            raise ValueError('loan limit reached')
        item.status, item.reserved_for = Status.LOANED, None
        loan = Loan(item, member, today + timedelta(days=self.LOAN_DAYS))
        self.loans[barcode] = loan
        return loan

    def reserve(self, member: str, book: Book): book.holds.append(member)

    def give_back(self, barcode: str, today: date) -> int:
        loan = self.loans.pop(barcode)
        fee = self.fine_policy.fine(loan.due, today)
        item = loan.item
        if item.book.holds:                           # next in line gets it
            item.status, item.reserved_for = Status.RESERVED, item.book.holds.popleft()
            self.notify(f'{item.reserved_for}: {item.book.title} is ready')
        else:
            item.status = Status.AVAILABLE
        return fee

lib = Library()
book = Book('9780132350884', 'Clean Code')
lib.add_copy(BookItem('BC-1', book))
d0 = date(2026, 1, 1)
lib.borrow('ravi', 'BC-1', d0)
lib.reserve('asha', book)
print(lib.give_back('BC-1', d0 + timedelta(days=17)))   # 30, and Asha is notified

lesson.complexity: Borrow/return are O(1) with maps keyed by barcode (the loan-limit check is O(loans) here — keep a per-member count to make it O(1)). Catalogue search needs an index by title/author.

topics.description: Book seats for a show without double booking: shows, seats, temporary seat holds with expiry and payments.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Movie Booking (BookMyShow) — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: browse movies by city → theatre → show; pick seats; pay; cancel.
2. Classes: `Movie`, `Theatre` → `Screen` → `Seat`; `Show` (movie + screen + time); `ShowSeat` (seat status **per show**); `Booking`; `PaymentService`; `PricingStrategy`.
3. **Hold → pay → confirm**: selected seats are LOCKED for a few minutes; unpaid holds expire back to AVAILABLE.
4. Concurrency: locking a set of seats must be all-or-nothing and atomic (lock / DB row locks / `UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE'`).

lesson.simple:
Users pick a movie, a show time and seats, then pay. The hard part is the one everybody asks about: **two people clicking the same seat at the same moment**.

The standard answer is a **two-step booking**:
1. **Hold** — when you select seats, they're **locked for you for ~5 minutes** (status LOCKED, with an expiry time).
2. **Confirm** — when payment succeeds, they become BOOKED. If you don't pay in time, the hold **expires** and the seats go back to AVAILABLE.

Modelling insight: a `Seat` belongs to a screen forever, but its *status* belongs to a specific **show**. So you need `ShowSeat` (show + seat + status).
lesson.analogy: Putting clothes on hold at a shop counter. The shopkeeper keeps them aside for you for 15 minutes. Pay in time and they're yours; walk away and they go back on the rack.

concepts.title: The domain hierarchy
concepts.body:
```text
City ─┬─ Theatre ─┬─ Screen ─── Seat (row, number, type: regular / premium / recliner)
      │           └─ Show (movie, screen, start time, language, format)
      └─ Movie (title, duration, languages, rating)

Show ─── ShowSeat (seat, price, status: AVAILABLE / LOCKED / BOOKED, holder, hold_until)
Booking (user, show, seats, amount, status: PENDING / CONFIRMED / CANCELLED, payment)
```

**Seat** is permanent furniture; **ShowSeat** is that seat *for one show*. Prices can differ per show and seat type (weekend evening premium), which is a `PricingStrategy` input. Browsing flows: city → movies showing → theatres and times → seat map for a show.

concepts.title: Hold, pay, confirm: the booking lifecycle
concepts.body:
1. **Select seats → hold.** Atomically move all selected ShowSeats from AVAILABLE (or expired LOCKED) to LOCKED for this user with `hold_until = now + 5 min`. All-or-nothing.
2. **Create a PENDING Booking** with the amount.
3. **Pay** through the payment gateway with an **idempotency key** (the booking id), outside any lock.
4. **Confirm.** Re-check that the seats are still LOCKED by this user and the hold hasn't expired; mark them BOOKED and the booking CONFIRMED.
5. **Failure paths:**
   - payment fails → release seats (or let them expire), booking CANCELLED;
   - payment succeeds but the hold expired and someone else booked → **automatic refund**;
   - user closes the app → hold expires on its own.

A background sweeper can reset expired locks, but treating an expired LOCKED seat as available at read time means correctness doesn't depend on the sweeper running.

concepts.title: Concurrency options compared
concepts.body:
| Approach | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **In-process lock** per show | `with show.lock:` | simple | only works on one server |
| **Pessimistic DB lock** | `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the seat rows, then update | correct, familiar | holds row locks; deadlock risk if seats are locked in different orders (sort seat ids!) |
| **Optimistic conditional update** | `UPDATE … WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE'`; check affected rows | no waiting, scales well | caller must handle "0 rows" and roll back |
| **Redis per-seat keys** | `SET seat:{show}:{id} user NX EX 300` | very fast, natural TTL | must keep Redis and DB in sync; multi-seat holds need a Lua script or rollback |

A strong answer: optimistic conditional update inside one transaction for the hold, idempotent payment, and a final conditional update for confirmation.

hints: In-memory locks only work on one machine.

items.explanation: Make the hold one atomic database statement that only succeeds if every seat is still free (or its hold expired), inside a transaction.
items.answer_md:
1. `BEGIN`
2. `UPDATE show_seats SET status='LOCKED', holder=:u, hold_until=now()+5m WHERE show_id=:s AND seat_id IN (:seats) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR hold_until < now())`
3. If affected rows ≠ seats requested → `ROLLBACK` (someone else got one).
4. `COMMIT`.

Alternatives: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (pessimistic), a `version` column (optimistic), or a Redis `SET seat:{show}:{id} user NX EX 300` per seat. Payment uses an idempotency key; the final `BOOKED` update re-checks the holder and expiry.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Car Rental — the shape of a good answer

1. Requirements: branches, vehicle types, search by location + date range, reserve, pick-up, return, late fees, add-ons.
2. Classes: `RentalSystem`, `Branch`, `Vehicle` (type, plate, status), `Reservation` (vehicle, from, to, state), `Customer`, `PricingStrategy`, `Payment`.
3. Availability = no existing reservation **overlaps** the requested range: `a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end`.
4. Reservation states: RESERVED → PICKED_UP → RETURNED (or CANCELLED / NO_SHOW).

lesson.simple:
Customers search for a car at a branch for certain dates, reserve it, pick it up, and return it later.

Unlike a parking spot, a car is booked for a **date range**, and the same car can have many future reservations. So "is this car free?" becomes: **does any existing reservation overlap the dates I want?**

The overlap rule is worth memorising: two ranges `[a_start, a_end)` and `[b_start, b_end)` overlap when **`a_start < b_end and b_start < a_end`**.

A `Reservation` moves through **states**: RESERVED → PICKED_UP → RETURNED (or CANCELLED). Pricing (daily rate × days, weekend surcharge, late fee) goes in a **PricingStrategy**.
lesson.analogy: A hotel room calendar: the same room can be booked by different guests for different weeks. Before saying yes, the receptionist checks the new dates don't cross any existing booking.

concepts.title: Availability as interval overlap
concepts.body:
A car is free for `[start, end)` if **no active reservation overlaps** that range. Two half-open ranges overlap exactly when:

```text
a_start < b_end  AND  b_start < a_end
```

Check the cases: touching ranges (`[5, 8)` and `[8, 10)`) don't overlap; containment, partial overlap from either side, and identical ranges all do.

**Performance:** checking every reservation is fine for a whiteboard. At scale:
- a DB index on `(vehicle_id, start_date)` plus the overlap condition,
- an **interval tree** per vehicle in memory,
- or Postgres's `daterange` with an **exclusion constraint** so the database itself refuses overlapping bookings — the strongest guarantee.

concepts.title: Search: from 'which cars?' to 'which car types?'
concepts.body:
Customers usually choose a **type** (hatchback, sedan, SUV), not a specific plate. So search answers: *"for branch B and dates D, which types have at least one free car, and at what price?"*

Two designs:
1. **Assign a specific car at booking time** — simple; check overlap per car.
2. **Book a type, assign a car at pickup** — more flexible (maintenance, late returns). Keep a count per (branch, type, date) like hotel inventory: booking increments `reserved` for each day if `reserved < total`. This is exactly the HLD hotel-reservation model.

Mention one-way rentals: availability then depends on cars arriving at a branch from returns, which pushes you towards option 2.

concepts.title: Reservation lifecycle and pricing
concepts.body:
```text
RESERVED ──pickup──▶ PICKED_UP ──return──▶ RETURNED ──pay──▶ CLOSED
   │                     │
 cancel               no-show (pickup window passed)
   ▼                     ▼
CANCELLED             NO_SHOW (fee)
```

Enforce transitions in one place (a `transition(to)` method that checks allowed moves), so an impossible history (RESERVED → RETURNED) can't happen.

**Pricing** composes nicely with Decorators: `BaseDailyRate → WeekendSurcharge → InsuranceAddOn → LateFee`. Each wraps the previous and adds its part, so new add-ons don't touch existing code. Store the **price quote** on the reservation at booking time; rate changes later shouldn't change what the customer agreed to.
